claim: Response inhibition is an essential component of cognitive control.
source: Response inhibition is an essential component of cognitive control.
evidence: This is a statement of established scientific understanding in the field of cognitive neuroscience.

claim: Attention deficit hyperactivity disorder demonstrates impaired response inhibition.
source: Many neuropsychiatric disorders like attention deficit hyperactivity disorder, obsessive-compulsive disorder, and Parkinson's disease demonstrate the severe impact of impaired response inhibition on mental health (Schachar and Logan, 1990; de Wit et al., 2012; Voon and Dalley, 2011).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous research studies.

claim: Obsessive-compulsive disorder demonstrates impaired response inhibition.
source: Many neuropsychiatric disorders like attention deficit hyperactivity disorder, obsessive-compulsive disorder, and Parkinson's disease demonstrate the severe impact of impaired response inhibition on mental health (Schachar and Logan, 1990; de Wit et al., 2012; Voon and Dalley, 2011).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous research studies.

claim: Parkinson's disease demonstrates impaired response inhibition.
source: Many neuropsychiatric disorders like attention deficit hyperactivity disorder, obsessive-compulsive disorder, and Parkinson's disease demonstrate the severe impact of impaired response inhibition on mental health (Schachar and Logan, 1990; de Wit et al., 2012; Voon and Dalley, 2011).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous research studies.

claim: The stop-signal task plays a major role in defining research on cognitive control.
source: Response inhibition has been operationalized via the classical stop-signal task (SST, Logan et al., 1984) in many studies; thus the SST plays a major role in defining research on cognitive control (Verbruggen et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citation to Verbruggen et al., 2019.

claim: The independent race model assumes the independence of go and stop processes.
source: A well-developed theoretical framework describing the cognitive processes underlying response inhibition relies on a so-called independent race model, which assumes the independence of go and stop processes (Logan et al., 1984; Verbruggen et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citations to Logan et al., 1984 and Verbruggen et al., 2019.

claim: Response inhibition crucially depends on the inferior frontal cortex.
source: So far, numerous studies using the SST provided consistent evidence that response inhibition crucially depends on two cortical regions: the inferior frontal cortex (IFC) and the pre-supplementary motor area (pre-SMA) (Wessel and Aron, 2017).
evidence: Supported by citation to Wessel and Aron, 2017.

claim: Response inhibition crucially depends on the pre-supplementary motor area.
source: So far, numerous studies using the SST provided consistent evidence that response inhibition crucially depends on two cortical regions: the inferior frontal cortex (IFC) and the pre-supplementary motor area (pre-SMA) (Wessel and Aron, 2017).
evidence: Supported by citation to Wessel and Aron, 2017.

claim: The functional roles of IFC and pre-SMA within response inhibition have been controversially debated for more than a decade.
source: The particular functional roles of these two regions within response inhibition have been controversially debated for more than a decade now (Aron et al., 2004; Hampshire and Sharp, 2015a; Aron et al., 2015; Hampshire and Sharp, 2015b).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations spanning over a decade.

claim: Some studies suggest that response inhibition is directly initiated by the IFC.
source: While a range of studies on response inhibition point toward a single inhibitory module within the IFC that directly initiates stopping (Aron et al., 2003), other studies assign this role to pre-SMA (Li et al., 2006; Nachev et al., 2007).
evidence: Supported by citation to Aron et al., 2003.

claim: Some studies assign the role of initiating stopping to pre-SMA.
source: While a range of studies on response inhibition point toward a single inhibitory module within the IFC that directly initiates stopping (Aron et al., 2003), other studies assign this role to pre-SMA (Li et al., 2006; Nachev et al., 2007).
evidence: Supported by citations to Li et al., 2006 and Nachev et al., 2007.

claim: Some authors suggest that the functional role of IFC within response inhibition is the encoding of context-specific task rules.
source: As an alternative, some authors suggest that the functional role of IFC within response inhibition is either the encoding of context-specific task rules or simply the attentional detection of the need for response inhibition, whereas its initiation is triggered by the pre-SMA (Duann et al., 2009; Sharp et al., 2010; Rae et al., 2015; Xu et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citations to multiple studies.

claim: Some authors suggest that the functional role of IFC within response inhibition is the attentional detection of the need for response inhibition.
source: As an alternative, some authors suggest that the functional role of IFC within response inhibition is either the encoding of context-specific task rules or simply the attentional detection of the need for response inhibition, whereas its initiation is triggered by the pre-SMA (Duann et al., 2009; Sharp et al., 2010; Rae et al., 2015; Xu et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citations to multiple studies.

claim: Some authors suggest that there is no unitary response inhibition module.
source: A more critical view questions the behavioral construct of response inhibition in general (Hampshire and Sharp, 2015a). Here, the authors suggest that there is no unitary response inhibition module and claim that the IFC is part of a domain-general control network (Erika-Florence et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citations to Hampshire and Sharp, 2015a and Erika-Florence et al., 2014.

claim: The temporal activation order of IFC and pre-SMA has become a decisive, yet unresolved question in the field.
source: However, in the attempts to experimentally define the differential roles of IFC and pre-SMA, the temporal activation order of those regions has become a decisive, yet unresolved question in the field (Allen et al., 2018; Swann et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citations to Allen et al., 2018 and Swann et al., 2012.

claim: One ECoG study in a single patient concluded that pre-SMA precedes the IFC activation.
source: One study used electrocorticography (ECoG) in a single patient and concluded that pre-SMA precedes the IFC activation (Swann et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citation to Swann et al., 2012.

claim: Two recent MEG studies suggest that IFC and pre-SMA may be simultaneously active with no temporal or functional primacy.
source: In contrast, two recent MEG studies suggest that both regions may be simultaneously active and that there is no temporal or functional primacy (Allen et al., 2018; Jha et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citations to Allen et al., 2018 and Jha et al., 2015.

claim: The selective stopping task comprises additional attentional capture go (AC-GO) trials that are identical to STOP trials in terms of timing and frequency.
source: To specifically control for the attentional load involved in the SST, Sharp et al., 2010 used a selective stopping task. This task comprises additional attentional capture go (AC-GO) trials that are identical to STOP trials in terms of timing and frequency, but participants have to continue with their already prepared go response (Figure 1A).
evidence: Supported by citation to Sharp et al., 2010 and reference to Figure 1A.

claim: Contrasting STOP versus AC-GO trials allows identification of the neural signature of response inhibition independently of other cognitive processes related to attention or conflict.
source: Contrasting both conditions (i.e., STOP versus AC-GO trials) has two main advantages. First, it allows us to identify the neural signature of response inhibition independently of other cognitive processes that are related to attention or conflict (Sharp et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by citation to Sharp et al., 2010.

claim: The race model assumes that in successful stop trials, the go process is slower than the stop process.
source: Note that the race model assumes that in sSTOP trials, the go process is slower than the stop process, while in uSTOP trials it is vice versa.
evidence: This is a statement about the theoretical framework of the race model.

claim: In unsuccessful stop trials, the go process is faster than the stop process.
source: Note that the race model assumes that in sSTOP trials, the go process is slower than the stop process, while in uSTOP trials it is vice versa.
evidence: This is a statement about the theoretical framework of the race model.

claim: Only three studies have used a selective stopping task with an AC-GO condition in connection with a high temporal resolution technique.
source: So far, to the best of our knowledge, only three studies used a selective stopping task with an AC-GO ('continue') condition in connection with a high temporal resolution technique.
evidence: This is a statement about the literature based on the authors' knowledge.

claim: Two studies used ECoG in patients with a selective stopping task.
source: Two studies used ECoG in a single patient (Swann et al., 2012), or in four patients (Wessel et al., 2013), respectively, but Wessel et al., 2013 could only cover the right IFC region, not pre-SMA.
evidence: Supported by citations to Swann et al., 2012 and Wessel et al., 2013.

claim: Wessel et al., 2013 could only cover the right IFC region, not pre-SMA.
source: Two studies used ECoG in a single patient (Swann et al., 2012), or in four patients (Wessel et al., 2013), respectively, but Wessel et al., 2013 could only cover the right IFC region, not pre-SMA.
evidence: Supported by citation to Wessel et al., 2013.

claim: Sánchez-Carmona et al., 2016 used EEG but did not analyze the temporal activation order of rIFG and pre-SMA.
source: Sánchez-Carmona et al., 2016 used EEG, but did not analyze the temporal activation order of both regions.
evidence: Supported by citation to Sánchez-Carmona et al., 2016.

claim: Previous findings suggest a predominant role of beta-band activity in rIFG and pre-SMA during stopping.
source: Based on previous findings, we hypothesized a predominant role of beta-band activity in both regions during the time of stopping (Kühn et al., 2004; Swann et al., 2009; Fonken et al., 2016) and aimed to define the temporal activation order and connectivity of IFC and pre-SMA during response inhibition.
evidence: Supported by citations to Kühn et al., 2004, Swann et al., 2009, and Fonken et al., 2016.

claim: The mean SSD was 294.5 ± 120.6 ms.
source: The mean SSD was 294.5 ± 120.6 ms (mean ± SD) and led to a probability of responding on a STOP trial close to 50% (49.0 ± 3.0%) proving the adherence of participants to the task rules and the successful operation of the staircase procedure (see 'Materials and methods' for more information).
evidence: This is a direct report of experimental data from the study.

claim: The probability of responding on a STOP trial was close to 50% (49.0 ± 3.0%).
source: The mean SSD was 294.5 ± 120.6 ms (mean ± SD) and led to a probability of responding on a STOP trial close to 50% (49.0 ± 3.0%) proving the adherence of participants to the task rules and the successful operation of the staircase procedure (see 'Materials and methods' for more information).
evidence: This is a direct report of experimental data from the study.

claim: The mean SSD for successful stop trials was 288.1 ± 124.6 ms.
source: While for sSTOP trials the mean SSD was 288.1 ± 124.6 ms, it was 300.9 ± 117.1 ms for uSTOP trials.
evidence: This is a direct report of experimental data from the study.

claim: The mean SSD for unsuccessful stop trials was 300.9 ± 117.1 ms.
source: While for sSTOP trials the mean SSD was 288.1 ± 124.6 ms, it was 300.9 ± 117.1 ms for uSTOP trials.
evidence: This is a direct report of experimental data from the study.

claim: The mean attentional capture signal delay for correct attentional capture go trials was 296.3 ± 118.4 ms.
source: The mean attentional capture signal delay (ACSD) for correct attentional capture go (cAC-GO) trials was 296.3 ± 118.4 ms.
evidence: This is a direct report of experimental data from the study.

claim: A repeated-measures ANOVA based on RT revealed a main effect of condition (F = 471.5, p<0.001).
source: A repeated-measures ANOVA based on RT revealed a main effect of condition (F = 471.5, p<0.001).
evidence: This is a direct report of statistical analysis results from the study.

claim: Mean RT in correct attentional capture go trials (588.2 ± 14.0 ms) was significantly longer compared to GO trials (550.2 ± 13.5 ms).
source: Bonferroni-corrected post hoc comparisons revealed that mean RT in cAC-GO trials (588.2 ± 14.0 ms, group mean ± standard error of the mean) was significantly longer as compared to GO trials (550.2 ± 13.5 ms) and uSTOP trials (499.6 ± 12.6 ms).
evidence: This is a direct report of statistical analysis results from the study.

claim: Mean RT in correct attentional capture go trials (588.2 ± 14.0 ms) was significantly longer compared to unsuccessful stop trials (499.6 ± 12.6 ms).
source: Bonferroni-corrected post hoc comparisons revealed that mean RT in cAC-GO trials (588.2 ± 14.0 ms, group mean ± standard error of the mean) was significantly longer as compared to GO trials (550.2 ± 13.5 ms) and uSTOP trials (499.6 ± 12.6 ms).
evidence: This is a direct report of statistical analysis results from the study.

claim: Mean RT in unsuccessful stop trials was significantly shorter compared to GO trials (p<0.001).
source: Mean RT in uSTOP trials was significantly shorter as compared to GO trials (p<0.001 for all post hoc tests; Figure 1C).
evidence: This is a direct report of statistical analysis results from the study, also shown in Figure 1C.

claim: Participants performed accurately with low omission error rates in GO trials (2.3 ± 2.8%).
source: Participants performed accurately as indicated by low omission error rates in GO (2.3 ± 2.8%, mean ± SD) and AC-GO trials (1.2 ± 1.4%).
evidence: This is a direct report of experimental data from the study.

claim: Participants performed accurately with low omission error rates in AC-GO trials (1.2 ± 1.4%).
source: Participants performed accurately as indicated by low omission error rates in GO (2.3 ± 2.8%, mean ± SD) and AC-GO trials (1.2 ± 1.4%).
evidence: This is a direct report of experimental data from the study.

claim: Accuracy was 97.2 ± 2.8% in GO trials.
source: Accuracy was 97.2 ± 2.8% in GO and 97.0 ± 2.8% in AC-GO trials (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is a direct report of experimental data from the study, also shown in Figure 1C.

claim: Accuracy was 97.0 ± 2.8% in AC-GO trials.
source: Accuracy was 97.2 ± 2.8% in GO and 97.0 ± 2.8% in AC-GO trials (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is a direct report of experimental data from the study, also shown in Figure 1C.

claim: The median SSRT was 244.2 ± 36.0 ms.
source: SSRT was calculated using the integration method (see 'Materials and methods' for more information), resulting in a median SSRT of 244.2 ± 36.0 ms.
evidence: This is a direct report of experimental data from the study.

claim: The maximal SSRT across participants was 349.9 ms.
source: The maximal SSRT across participants (SSRTmax) was 349.9 ms.
evidence: This is a direct report of experimental data from the study.

claim: There was no interaction between signal color and RT (GO versus AC-GO) (F = 0.847, p = 0.361).
source: A mixed-design ANOVA with signal color as between factor and RT (GO versus AC-GO) as within factor further revealed no influence of attribution of color to trial type, as no interaction of these two factors was present (F = 0.847, p = 0.361).
evidence: This is a direct report of statistical analysis results from the study.

claim: Beta-band power was increased in successful stop compared to correct attentional capture go trials in a network of pre-motor and pre-frontal areas.
source: This contrast revealed that beta-band power was increased in sSTOP compared to cAC-GO trials in a network of pre-motor and pre-frontal areas (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is a direct report of experimental results from the study, shown in Figure 2A.

claim: One main cluster of increased beta-band power was located in the IFC with its maximum in the right inferior frontal gyrus, pars opercularis.
source: One main cluster of increased beta-band power was located in the IFC with its maximum in the right inferior frontal gyrus (rIFG), pars opercularis.
evidence: This is a direct report of experimental results from the study.

claim: Increased beta-band power was present in the pre-SMA, left middle frontal gyrus, and bilateral premotor regions.
source: Increased beta-band power was also present in the pre-SMA, left middle frontal gyrus (lMFG), and bilateral premotor regions (Table 1, Figure 2A).
evidence: This is a direct report of experimental results from the study, shown in Table 1 and Figure 2A.

claim: The same analysis performed for the gamma band did not reveal a significant cluster.
source: The same analysis performed for the gamma band did not reveal a significant cluster.
evidence: This is a direct report of experimental results from the study.

claim: In fMRI, the contrast sSTOP versus cAC-GO revealed broad activation of bilateral prefrontal, sensorimotor, parietal, and occipital areas.
source: Here, the contrast sSTOP versus cAC-GO revealed broad activation of bilateral prefrontal, sensorimotor, parietal, and occipital areas (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is a direct report of experimental results from the fMRI study, shown in Figure 2B.

claim: In fMRI, rIFG was activated in two subregions: pars triangularis (BA45, x = 52, y = 22, z = 4, t = 10.96) and pars opercularis (BA44, x = 52, y = 18, z = 14, t = 9.42).
source: In particular, rIFG was activated in two subregions (pars triangularis, BA45, x = 52, y = 22, z = 4, t = 10.96; pars opercularis, BA44, x = 52, y = 18, z = 14, t = 9.42), while pre-SMA (x = 16, y = 14, z = 64, t = 9.45) was identified as sub-maxima in the biggest cluster obtained (13,438 voxels) as well as in a smaller cluster (85 voxels) (x = –‍14, y = 18, z = 66, t = 5.63).
evidence: This is a direct report of experimental results from the fMRI study.

claim: In fMRI, pre-SMA (x = 16, y = 14, z = 64, t = 9.45) was identified as sub-maxima in the biggest cluster obtained (13,438 voxels).
source: In particular, rIFG was activated in two subregions (pars triangularis, BA45, x = 52, y = 22, z = 4, t = 10.96; pars opercularis, BA44, x = 52, y = 18, z = 14, t = 9.42), while pre-SMA (x = 16, y = 14, z = 64, t = 9.45) was identified as sub-maxima in the biggest cluster obtained (13,438 voxels) as well as in a smaller cluster (85 voxels) (x = –‍14, y = 18, z = 66, t = 5.63).
evidence: This is a direct report of experimental results from the fMRI study.

claim: The comparison of activity revealed by the MEG and fMRI contrasts showed an overall good correspondence.
source: The comparison of activity revealed by the MEG and fMRI contrasts showed an overall good correspondence.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the comparison between MEG and fMRI results.

claim: The distance between peaks of both methods were rather close for rIFG (7 mm).
source: Given the 1 cm grid used for the MEG source reconstruction, the distance between peaks of both methods were rather close for rIFG (7 mm), pre-SMA (15 mm), lAIns (11 mm), and lMFG (15 mm).
evidence: This is a direct report of the comparison between MEG and fMRI results.

claim: The distance between peaks of both methods were rather close for pre-SMA (15 mm).
source: Given the 1 cm grid used for the MEG source reconstruction, the distance between peaks of both methods were rather close for rIFG (7 mm), pre-SMA (15 mm), lAIns (11 mm), and lMFG (15 mm).
evidence: This is a direct report of the comparison between MEG and fMRI results.

claim: The earliest beta-band power difference was found in the rIFG source compared to all other sources.
source: The earliest beta-band power difference was found in the rIFG source compared to all other sources (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is a direct report of experimental results from the study, shown in Figure 3C.

claim: A permutation test revealed a significant latency onset difference between rIFG and pre-SMA (p=0.0240, two-tailed test).
source: These onsets were then used as input for a permutation test that revealed a significant latency onset difference between both sources (p=0.0240, two-tailed test, mean onset latency rIFG: 137 ± 46 ms, and pre-SMA: 159 ± 52 ms).
evidence: This is a direct report of statistical analysis results from the study.

claim: Mean onset latency for rIFG was 137 ± 46 ms.
source: These onsets were then used as input for a permutation test that revealed a significant latency onset difference between both sources (p=0.0240, two-tailed test, mean onset latency rIFG: 137 ± 46 ms, and pre-SMA: 159 ± 52 ms).
evidence: This is a direct report of experimental results from the study.

claim: Mean onset latency for pre-SMA was 159 ± 52 ms.
source: These onsets were then used as input for a permutation test that revealed a significant latency onset difference between both sources (p=0.0240, two-tailed test, mean onset latency rIFG: 137 ± 46 ms, and pre-SMA: 159 ± 52 ms).
evidence: This is a direct report of experimental results from the study.

claim: The SVM-based approach revealed a robust above-chance level classification starting from 129 ms (p<0.0001) after STOP/AC-GO signal onset for the rIFG source.
source: This SVM-based approach revealed a robust above-chance level classification starting from 129 ms (p<0.0001) after STOP/AC-GO signal onset for the rIFG source and from 163 ms (p<0.0001) for the pre-SMA source (Figure 4A, tested within tROI, 100–350 ms).
evidence: This is a direct report of statistical analysis results from the study, shown in Figure 4A.

claim: The SVM-based approach revealed a robust above-chance level classification starting from 163 ms (p<0.0001) for the pre-SMA source.
source: This SVM-based approach revealed a robust above-chance level classification starting from 129 ms (p<0.0001) after STOP/AC-GO signal onset for the rIFG source and from 163 ms (p<0.0001) for the pre-SMA source (Figure 4A, tested within tROI, 100–350 ms).
evidence: This is a direct report of statistical analysis results from the study, shown in Figure 4A.

claim: The analysis showed a significantly earlier rIFG onset compared to pre-SMA at a threshold of 25% with p=0.0377.
source: This analysis showed a significantly earlier rIFG onset compared to pre-SMA at a threshold of 25% with p=0.0377 (p=0.0062).
evidence: This is a direct report of statistical analysis results from the study.

claim: Mean onset in rIFG was 178 ms (186 ms) and 200 ms (220 ms) in pre-SMA.
source: Mean onset in rIFG was 178 ms (186 ms) and 200 ms (220 ms) in pre-SMA (first value refers to an analysis that relied on classification peaks with an accuracy above one standard deviation of the mean baseline accuracy, while the second value in parentheses refers to two standard deviations).
evidence: This is a direct report of experimental results from the study.

claim: Accuracy was significantly above chance level in the rIFG at 132 ms (p<0.0001) using beta-band filtered data.
source: Accuracy was significantly above chance level in the rIFG at 132 ms (p<0.0001) and in pre-SMA at 142 ms (p<0.0001), tested within tROI (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is a direct report of statistical analysis results from the study, shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Accuracy was significantly above chance level in pre-SMA at 142 ms (p<0.0001) using beta-band filtered data.
source: Accuracy was significantly above chance level in the rIFG at 132 ms (p<0.0001) and in pre-SMA at 142 ms (p<0.0001), tested within tROI (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is a direct report of statistical analysis results from the study, shown in Figure 4B.

claim: The beta-band filtered data allowed to reliably classify successful stop trials, indicating that beta-band oscillations are carrying the crucial information to reliably classify successful stop trials.
source: Yet, the beta-band filtered data allowed to reliably classify sSTOP trials, indicating that beta-band oscillations are carrying the crucial information to reliably classify sSTOP trials.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the SVM analysis results on beta-band filtered data.

claim: In the winning model 3, there was a 91% marginal posterior probability for a negative regression coefficient of the beta power in rIFG for successful trials.
source: In the winning model 3, there was as 91% marginal posterior probability for a negative regression coefficient of the beta power in rIFG for successful trials, and a 87% marginal posterior probability for a negative regression coefficient for the DAI, but only a 64% marginal posterior probability for a negative regression coefficient for the average beta power in pre-SMA, and a 40% marginal posterior probability for a negative regression coefficient for the beta power in rIFG in failed trials (for more details, consult the linked notebook in Box 1).
evidence: This is a direct report of statistical analysis results from the Bayesian regression.

claim: In the winning model 3, there was a 87% marginal posterior probability for a negative regression coefficient for the DAI.
source: In the winning model 3, there was as 91% marginal posterior probability for a negative regression coefficient of the beta power in rIFG for successful trials, and a 87% marginal posterior probability for a negative regression coefficient for the DAI, but only a 64% marginal posterior probability for a negative regression coefficient for the average beta power in pre-SMA, and a 40% marginal posterior probability for a negative regression coefficient for the beta power in rIFG in failed trials (for more details, consult the linked notebook in Box 1).
evidence: This is a direct report of statistical analysis results from the Bayesian regression.

claim: Beta power in rIFG in successful trials and the DAI predict SSRT outcomes.
source: Given these results, we consider it most plausible that beta power in rIFG in successful trials and the DAI predict SSRT outcomes, with all other regressors having no or a much smaller influence.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the Bayesian regression results.

claim: The cluster-based permutation test revealed statistical differences between successful stop and correct attentional capture go conditions within the (high) beta band in the direction rIFG to pre-SMA (pcluster = 0.0074, corrected for the two links tested).
source: The cluster-based permutation test (see 'Materials and methods' for more information) revealed statistical differences between sSTOP and cAC-GO conditions within the (high) beta band in the direction rIFG to pre-SMA (pcluster = 0.0074, corrected for the two links tested), but not in the opposite direction (Figure 5A).
evidence: This is a direct report of statistical analysis results from the connectivity analysis, shown in Figure 5A.

claim: The cluster-based permutation test did not reveal statistical differences in the direction pre-SMA to rIFG.
source: The cluster-based permutation test (see 'Materials and methods' for more information) revealed statistical differences between sSTOP and cAC-GO conditions within the (high) beta band in the direction rIFG to pre-SMA (pcluster = 0.0074, corrected for the two links tested), but not in the opposite direction (Figure 5A).
evidence: This is a direct report of statistical analysis results from the connectivity analysis, shown in Figure 5A.

claim: The better subjects were able to inhibit their response (faster SSRT), the higher, positive DAI values they had, indicating a stronger connectivity from rIFG to pre-SMA.
source: Hence, the better subjects were able to inhibit their response, that is, the faster their SSRT was, the higher, positive DAI values they had, indicating a stronger connectivity from rIFG to pre-SMA, whereas slower inhibiting subjects showed the reverse pattern (negative DAI, stronger connectivity from pre-SMA to rIFG, Figure 5B).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the correlation between DAI and SSRT, shown in Figure 5B.

claim: Slower inhibiting subjects showed the reverse pattern (negative DAI, stronger connectivity from pre-SMA to rIFG).
source: Hence, the better subjects were able to inhibit their response, that is, the faster their SSRT was, the higher, positive DAI values they had, indicating a stronger connectivity from rIFG to pre-SMA, whereas slower inhibiting subjects showed the reverse pattern (negative DAI, stronger connectivity from pre-SMA to rIFG, Figure 5B).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the correlation between DAI and SSRT, shown in Figure 5B.

claim: The asymmetry of communication between rIFG and pre-SMA affects the stopping process.
source: This demonstrates that the asymmetry of communication between rIFG and pre-SMA affects the stopping process.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the correlation between DAI and SSRT.

claim: The sliding window analysis revealed decrease in rIFG to pre-SMA connectivity in two additional windows.
source: This post hoc analysis revealed decrease in rIFG to pre-SMA connectivity in two additional windows.
evidence: This is a direct report of the sliding window analysis results.

claim: In the first additional time window from 200 to 450 ms, the flanks of the beta band showed a difference in cGC between conditions.
source: In the first additional time window from 200 to 450 ms, the flanks of the beta band showed a difference in cGC between conditions. Note that this first effect was not significant after the correction for multiple comparisons of six time windows and of each direction tested (p(lower cluster) = 0.0052, p(upper cluster) = 0.0207, both uncorrected).
evidence: This is a direct report of the sliding window analysis results.

claim: In a second, later window (300–550 ms), the upper flank of the beta band showed a significant difference between conditions (p(upper cluster) = 0.0384, corrected).
source: However, in a second, later window (300–550 ms), the upper flank of the beta band showed a significant difference between conditions (p(upper cluster) = 0.0384, corrected, and p(lower cluster) = 0.0064, uncorrected).
evidence: This is a direct report of the sliding window analysis results.

claim: No significant differences were found in any time window before the tROI and after 550 ms, nor in the direction of pre-SMA to rIFG.
source: No significant differences were found in any time window before the tROI and after 550 ms, nor in the direction of pre-SMA to rIFG.
evidence: This is a direct report of the sliding window analysis results.

claim: Response inhibition is initiated within a crucial time range by specific rIFG to pre-SMA connectivity, the strength of which correlates with behavioral performance.
source: Overall, our cGC findings suggest that response inhibition is initiated within a crucial time range by specific rIFG to pre-SMA connectivity, the strength of which correlates with behavioral performance.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the connectivity analysis results.

claim: This study is the first to show a significantly earlier activation in the rIFG compared to the pre-SMA using high temporal resolution MEG and a relatively large cohort of subjects.
source: Our study, using the high temporal resolution of MEG and a relatively large cohort of subjects, is the first to show a significantly earlier activation in the rIFG compared to the pre-SMA.
evidence: This is a claim about the novelty of the study's findings.

claim: The onset of beta-band activity in the rIFG was found at ∼140 ms after the STOP signal.
source: The onset of beta-band activity in the rIFG was found at ∼140 ms after the STOP signal, which is in the same range (∼120 ms) as revealed by an independent component analysis (ICA) of a recent EEG study (Jana et al., 2020).
evidence: This is a direct report of experimental results from the study, supported by citation to Jana et al., 2020.

claim: The onset of beta-band activity in the pre-SMA started at least 22 ms later than rIFG.
source: The onset of beta-band activity in the pre-SMA started at least 22 ms later – as independently verified by a latency analysis of spectral power and a time-resolved SVM analysis.
evidence: This is a direct report of experimental results from the study.

claim: Connectivity analysis showed that rIFG sends information in the beta band for successful stopping to pre-SMA but not vice versa.
source: Connectivity analysis showed that rIFG sends information in the beta band for successful stopping to pre-SMA but not vice versa.
evidence: This is a direct report of experimental results from the study.

claim: The behavioral significance of beta-band power in rIFG was demonstrated by its prediction of stopping performance.
source: The behavioral significance of beta-band power in rIFG as well as of the connectivity from rIFG to pre-SMA in the beta band was demonstrated by their prediction of stopping performance.
evidence: This is a direct report of experimental results from the study.

claim: The behavioral significance of connectivity from rIFG to pre-SMA in the beta band was demonstrated by its prediction of stopping performance.
source: The behavioral significance of beta-band power in rIFG as well as of the connectivity from rIFG to pre-SMA in the beta band was demonstrated by their prediction of stopping performance.
evidence: This is a direct report of experimental results from the study.

claim: Two previous MEG studies reported that the pre-SMA and rIFG were simultaneously activated in the time window between STOP signal and SSRT.
source: Two of these studies (Allen et al., 2018; Jha et al., 2015) reported that the pre-SMA and rIFG were simultaneously activated in the time window between STOP signal and SSRT.
evidence: Supported by citations to Allen et al., 2018 and Jha et al., 2015.

claim: SSRT was better predicted by the beta-band power of successful trials in rIFG compared to pre-SMA.
source: Indeed, SSRT was better predicted by the beta-band power of successful trials in rIFG compared to pre-SMA.
evidence: This is a direct report of experimental results from the study.

claim: In the rIFG, the beta-band power of successful trials was negatively correlated with the SSRT.
source: In the rIFG, the beta-band power of successful trials was negatively correlated with the SSRT.
evidence: This is a direct report of experimental results from the study.

claim: Several fMRI studies found a negative correlation between rIFG activation and SSRT.
source: This is in line with several fMRI studies, where a negative correlation between rIFG activation and SSRT was found (Aron and Poldrack, 2006; Aron et al., 2007; Rubia et al., 2007), suggesting that subjects with greater activation in rIFG inhibited more quickly (shorter SSRT).
evidence: Supported by citations to Aron and Poldrack, 2006, Aron et al., 2007, and Rubia et al., 2007.

claim: Recent EEG/TMS studies found that the timing of beta bursts correlated with SSRT.
source: More importantly, this relationship was also revealed by recent EEG/transcranial magnetic stimulation (TMS) studies (Hannah et al., 2020; Sundby et al., 2021), which found that the timing of beta bursts correlated with SSRT.
evidence: Supported by citations to Hannah et al., 2020 and Sundby et al., 2021.

claim: Both successful stop and unsuccessful stop trials had the same temporal activation pattern, that is, rIFG before pre-SMA.
source: Notably, both, sSTOP and uSTOP, trials had the same temporal activation pattern, that is, rIFG before pre-SMA.
evidence: This is a direct report of experimental results from the study.

claim: In successful stop trials, the rIFG beta-band power predicted the SSRT better than in unsuccessful stop trials.
source: However, in the sSTOP trials, the rIFG beta-band power predicted the SSRT better than in the uSTOP trials.
evidence: This is a direct report of experimental results from the study.

claim: The temporal precedence of rIFG over pre-SMA may be relevant for stopping in general, while the degree of control by the rIFG is responsible for the success and the performance of stopping.
source: Hence, the temporal precedence of rIFG over pre-SMA may indeed be relevant for stopping in general, while at the same time, the degree of control by the rIFG is responsible for the success and the performance of stopping.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the experimental results.

claim: A significant difference between successful stop and correct attentional capture go in conditional Granger causality influence from rIFG to pre-SMA was detected.
source: Indeed, a significant difference between sSTOP and cAC-GO in cGC influence from rIFG to pre-SMA was detected, but not in the opposite direction.
evidence: This is a direct report of experimental results from the study.

claim: The observed directionality is in line with conditional Granger causality analysis in a comparably high-powered fMRI study.
source: The observed directionality is in line with cGCA in a comparably high-powered fMRI study (Duann et al., 2009) (n = 57), yet inconsistent with GCA of a somewhat lower powered MEG study (Allen et al., 2018) (n = 19).
evidence: Supported by citations to Duann et al., 2009 and Allen et al., 2018.

claim: A recent DCM analysis of an EEG study found (inhibitory) connectivity from rIFG to pre-SMA during STOP trials to be negatively related to SSRT when transcranial focused ultrasound was applied.
source: This is compatible with a recent DCM (dynamic causal modeling) analysis of an EEG study available in preprint (Fine et al., 2019) that also found (inhibitory) connectivity from rIFG to pre-SMA during STOP trials to be negatively related to SSRT when transcranial focused ultrasound was applied.
evidence: Supported by citation to Fine et al., 2019.

claim: Connectivity directed from rIFG to pre-SMA per se reflects a state in which rIFG is prepared to send a signal to pre-SMA to execute stopping.
source: These findings suggest that connectivity directed from rIFG to pre-SMA per se reflects a state in which rIFG is prepared to send a signal to pre-SMA to execute stopping, while the strength of this directionality influences the performance of stopping.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the connectivity analysis results.

claim: The strength of directionality from rIFG to pre-SMA influences the performance of stopping.
source: These findings suggest that connectivity directed from rIFG to pre-SMA per se reflects a state in which rIFG is prepared to send a signal to pre-SMA to execute stopping, while the strength of this directionality influences the performance of stopping.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the connectivity analysis results.

claim: Inhibition-related beta-band connectivity between rIFG and pre-SMA was specific to the tROI and a subsequent time window, particularly only in the direction from rIFG to pre-SMA.
source: Thus, we could confirm that inhibition-related beta-band connectivity between rIFG and pre-SMA was specific to the tROI and a subsequent time window, particularly only in the direction from rIFG to pre-SMA.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the sliding window analysis results.

claim: rIFG may be characterized as a brake in response inhibition.
source: Since connectivity from rIFG to pre-SMA was specifically established during the tROI and correlated with inhibitory performance, rIFG may be characterized as a brake in response inhibition.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the connectivity analysis results.

claim: This interpretation is in line with Aron et al., 2014.
source: This interpretation is in line with Aron et al., 2014 and was recently corroborated by an ECoG study that revealed evidence for the prefrontal-subthalamic hyperdirect pathway, where stopping-related potentials in the rIFG preceded the ones in the subthalamic nucleus (STN) (Chen et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citations to Aron et al., 2014 and Chen et al., 2020.

claim: An ECoG study revealed evidence for the prefrontal-subthalamic hyperdirect pathway, where stopping-related potentials in the rIFG preceded the ones in the subthalamic nucleus.
source: This interpretation is in line with Aron et al., 2014 and was recently corroborated by an ECoG study that revealed evidence for the prefrontal-subthalamic hyperdirect pathway, where stopping-related potentials in the rIFG preceded the ones in the subthalamic nucleus (STN) (Chen et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citation to Chen et al., 2020.

claim: The rIFG signals the need to stop an already initiated action in the sense that it triggers a cascade of events that ultimately results in action cancelation.
source: Our results strongly support the interpretation that the rIFG signals the need to stop an already initiated action in the sense that it triggers a cascade of events that ultimately results in action cancelation and that beta-band oscillations are critically involved in this process.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the study's results.

claim: Beta-band oscillations are critically involved in the process of response inhibition.
source: Our results strongly support the interpretation that the rIFG signals the need to stop an already initiated action in the sense that it triggers a cascade of events that ultimately results in action cancelation and that beta-band oscillations are critically involved in this process.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the study's results.

claim: Beta-band oscillations are thought to be related to the maintenance of the current sensorimotor or cognitive state.
source: In general, beta-band oscillations are thought to be related to the maintenance of the current sensorimotor or cognitive state as hypothesized by a prominent model (Engel and Fries, 2010).
evidence: Supported by citation to Engel and Fries, 2010.

claim: Desynchronization of beta-band oscillations enables the transition into an active processing state.
source: In contrast, desynchronization of beta-band oscillations enables the transition into an active processing state (Miller et al., 2012; Little et al., 2019), for example, pressing a button.
evidence: Supported by citations to Miller et al., 2012 and Little et al., 2019.

claim: Beta-band desynchronization is related to motor response preparation.
source: Our TFR results can be explained within the framework of this model, that is, beta-band desynchronization (BBD) is related to motor response preparation and BBD should already set in early, after the initial GO signal.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the TFR results within the framework of the beta-band oscillation model.

claim: Until approximately 100 ms after the STOP/AC-GO signal, almost the same strength of beta-band desynchronization was observed for both conditions.
source: And indeed, until approximately 100 ms after the STOP/AC-GO signal, we observe almost the same strength of BBD for both conditions (so that it cancels out in the contrast, Figure 3C).
evidence: This is a direct report of experimental results from the study, shown in Figure 3C.

claim: In correct attentional capture go trials, the beta-band desynchronization continues until the median RT in the rIFG.
source: While in cAC-GO trials, the BBD continues until the median RT in the rIFG (Figure 3B, D), BBD is aborted in sSTOP trials already before the median SSRT, as we see an increase of beta-band power (Figure 3A, D).
evidence: This is a direct report of experimental results from the study, shown in Figures 3B and 3D.

claim: Beta-band desynchronization is aborted in successful stop trials already before the median SSRT, as an increase of beta-band power is observed.
source: While in cAC-GO trials, the BBD continues until the median RT in the rIFG (Figure 3B, D), BBD is aborted in sSTOP trials already before the median SSRT, as we see an increase of beta-band power (Figure 3A, D).
evidence: This is a direct report of experimental results from the study, shown in Figures 3A and 3D.

claim: As soon as the stopping or motor response is completed, beta-band oscillations resynchronize.
source: As soon as the stopping or motor response, respectively, is completed, beta-band oscillations resynchronize (Fonken et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citation to Fonken et al., 2016.

claim: In the rIFG, there was a rather early termination of beta-band desynchronization in successful stop trials in the sense that beta-band power started to increase shortly after the STOP signal.
source: Yet, what we found in the rIFG was a rather early termination of BBD in sSTOP trials in the sense that beta-band power started to increase shortly after the STOP signal (Figure 3D).
evidence: This is a direct report of experimental results from the study, shown in Figure 3D.

claim: The relative change in beta power found in the contrast originates genuinely in the successful stop trials, where beta-band desynchronization is terminated early.
source: Thus, the relative change in beta power that we found in the contrast originates genuinely in the sSTOP trials, where BBD is terminated early, that is, before the SSRT, while in the cAC-GO trials no such termination was observed.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the experimental results.

claim: This finding suggests an active change of processing in rIFG that is related to stopping, while processing proceeds 'as usual' in correct attentional capture go trials.
source: This finding suggests an active change of processing in rIFG that is related to stopping, while processing proceeds 'as usual' in cAC-GO trials, and the motor response will be executed.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the experimental results.

claim: The finding of significant Granger causality in time windows relevant for stopping, but not earlier, suggests that active signaling from rIFG to pre-SMA specifically in the beta band is an important part of the neural dynamics underlying stopping.
source: Furthermore, while we are fully aware that absence of evidence is not evidence of absence, the finding of significant Granger causality in time windows relevant for stopping, but not earlier, suggests that active signaling from rIFG to pre-SMA specifically in the beta band is an important part of the neural dynamics underlying stopping.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the connectivity analysis results.

claim: Response inhibition is implemented in part by beta-band modulations.
source: In sum, the two findings, that is, rIFG as source of stopping relevant information transfer in the beta band and a termination of BBD specifically in rIFG already before SSRT, suggest that response inhibition is implemented in part by beta-band modulations.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the study's results.

claim: Evidence from previous research indicates that the stopping process is related to a modulation of oscillatory power in the beta band.
source: Although the present data and evidence from previous research (Wessel et al., 2013; Castiglione et al., 2019) indicate that the stopping process is related to a modulation of oscillatory power in the beta band, it still needs to be determined whether beta changes result from a pausing of action initiation or whether they have a genuine stopping function.
evidence: Supported by citations to Wessel et al., 2013 and Castiglione et al., 2019.

claim: It still needs to be determined whether beta changes result from a pausing of action initiation or whether they have a genuine stopping function.
source: Although the present data and evidence from previous research (Wessel et al., 2013; Castiglione et al., 2019) indicate that the stopping process is related to a modulation of oscillatory power in the beta band, it still needs to be determined whether beta changes result from a pausing of action initiation or whether they have a genuine stopping function.
evidence: This is a statement about the limitations of current understanding.

claim: Contrasting successful stop with unsuccessful stop trials involves error processing.
source: Contrasting sSTOP with uSTOP trials, for example, involves error processing (Rubia et al., 2003) and an early response in motor cortices that has the potential to obscure activity related to the adjacent pre-SMA (Allen et al., 2018; Jerbi et al., 2007).
evidence: Supported by citations to Rubia et al., 2003, Allen et al., 2018, and Jerbi et al., 2007.

claim: Contrasting successful stop with unsuccessful stop trials was criticized as overly conservative because it assumes that inhibitory processes are also present in unsuccessful stop trials.
source: Additionally, this contrast was criticized as overly conservative, because it assumes that inhibitory processes are also present in uSTOP trials (Boehler et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by citation to Boehler et al., 2010.

claim: A less frequent event like the STOP signal is perceptually more salient and causes significant brain activation that is not directly based on inhibitory processing alone.
source: First, a less frequent event like the STOP signal is perceptually more salient and causes significant brain activation that is not directly based on inhibitory processing alone (Sharp et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by citation to Sharp et al., 2010.

claim: STOP signals are delayed compared to the GO signals, hence directly contrasting both trial types entails the comparison of different time points within the stopping process.
source: Second, STOP signals are delayed compared to the GO signals (i.e., SSD), hence directly contrasting both trial types entails the comparison of different time points within the stopping process (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is a statement about the task design, illustrated in Figure 1A.

claim: Attentional and discriminative processing of the STOP signal are presumed to disturb the timing of go and stop processes compared to GO trials.
source: Additionally, attentional and discriminative processing of the STOP signal are presumed to disturb the timing of go and stop processes compared to GO trials (Sharp et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by citation to Sharp et al., 2010.

claim: The contrast successful stop versus correct attentional capture go is the most appropriate to identify the neural correlates of 'pure' response inhibition, independent of attentional and error processing.
source: Hence, the contrast sSTOP versus cAC-GO is the most appropriate to identify the neural correlates of 'pure' response inhibition, independent of attentional and error processing (Sánchez-Carmona et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citation to Sánchez-Carmona et al., 2016.

claim: The dissociation of inhibitory from attentional processes by an appropriate task design suggests that the rIFG does not, at least not primarily, serve an attentional role in response inhibition.
source: The dissociation of inhibitory from attentional processes by an appropriate task design suggests that the rIFG does not, at least not primarily, serve an attentional role in response inhibition.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the study's results.

claim: The rIFG might still be part of a more domain-general cognitive control mechanism, implemented by frontoparietal networks.
source: However, although the rIFG has often been regarded as candidate for an inhibitory module and our results showed that response inhibition is indeed initiated by the rIFG, the rIFG might still be part of a more domain-general cognitive control mechanism, implemented by frontoparietal networks (Erika-Florence et al., 2014; Hampshire and Sharp, 2015a).
evidence: Supported by citations to Erika-Florence et al., 2014 and Hampshire and Sharp, 2015a.

claim: This study could not analyze activity of the STN because MEG is less sensitive to subcortical compared to cortical sources.
source: One limitation of this study is that we could not analyze activity of the STN which is an important subcortical node within the response inhibition network because of its direct relation to IFG (Aron et al., 2007; Duann et al., 2009; Jahfari et al., 2011; Rae et al., 2015; Xu et al., 2017; Chen et al., 2020). No STN activity was detected by our source reconstruction contrast, most likely because MEG is less sensitive to subcortical compared to cortical sources (Gross, 2019).
evidence: Supported by citations to multiple studies and Gross, 2019.

claim: Several studies with intracranial recordings detected beta-band oscillations within the STN.
source: Nonetheless, several studies with intracranial recordings detected beta-band oscillations within the STN (Kühn et al., 2004; Ray et al., 2012; Zavala et al., 2018; Fischer et al., 2018; Chen et al., 2020), also supporting the importance of beta-band oscillations in response inhibition.
evidence: Supported by citations to multiple studies.

claim: The findings strongly support the hypothesis that response inhibition is initiated by the rIFG and implemented as a top-down control via beta-band oscillations.
source: Our findings strongly support the hypothesis that response inhibition is initiated by the rIFG and implemented as a top-down control via beta-band oscillations (Aron et al., 2014).
evidence: This is a summary of the study's main findings, supported by citation to Aron et al., 2014.

claim: This brake is turned on in a time window around 100–200 ms after the STOP signal.
source: This brake is turned on in a time window around 100–200 ms after the STOP signal.
evidence: This is a summary of the study's findings on timing.

claim: Within the framework of the race model, rIFG may promote stopping processes and then signals to pre-SMA, among other regions, to proceed and execute the stopping process.
source: Within the framework of the race model, rIFG may promote stopping processes and then signals to pre-SMA, among other regions, to proceed and execute the stopping process.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the study's findings within the race model framework.

claim: Due to the task design, contrasting successful stop with correct attentional capture go trials, the study could exclude a primarily attentional role of the rIFG in stopping.
source: Due to our task design, that is, contrasting sSTOP with cAC-GO trials, we could exclude a primarily attentional role of the rIFG in stopping.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the study's results.

claim: These results may open up new ways of spatially localized oscillation-based interventions, that is, modulating beta-band activity by real-time EEG-triggered TMS.
source: Thus, these results may open up new ways of spatially localized oscillation-based interventions, that is, modulating beta-band activity by real-time EEG-triggered TMS.
evidence: This is a speculation about potential applications of the findings.

claim: Additional causal evidence for the mechanisms of response inhibition may open up new avenues of novel therapeutic strategies for diseases related to impaired response inhibition.
source: Additional causal evidence for the mechanisms of response inhibition may open up new avenues of novel therapeutic strategies for diseases related to impaired response inhibition.
evidence: This is a speculation about potential applications of the findings.

claim: Sixty-two healthy subjects participated in the MEG experiment.
source: Sixty-two healthy subjects participated in the MEG experiment.
evidence: This is a direct report of the study's methods.

claim: Three participants were excluded from the MEG experiment, resulting in 59 participants for analysis.
source: As a result of applying behavioral outlier criteria (Congdon et al., 2012), one participant had to be excluded because the inhibition stop rate was below 40%. A second participant had to be excluded because the mean RT of uSTOP trials was higher than the mean RT of cGO trials, indicating that the assumptions underlying the horse race model (Logan et al., 1984) were violated in this participant. A third participant had to be excluded because no head model could be obtained from the available anatomical MR image. All of the remaining 59 participants (39 women; mean age ± SD, 25 ± 6 years) had normal or corrected-to-normal vision.
evidence: This is a direct report of the study's methods and participant exclusions.

claim: A subset of 31 participants of the MEG experiment performed the fMRI task.
source: A subset of 31 participants of the MEG experiment performed the fMRI task and additionally data from 45 participants from the Sebastian et al., 2017 study were included for analysis (n = 76).
evidence: This is a direct report of the study's methods.

claim: Data from 45 participants from the Sebastian et al., 2017 study were included for fMRI analysis, resulting in n = 76.
source: A subset of 31 participants of the MEG experiment performed the fMRI task and additionally data from 45 participants from the Sebastian et al., 2017 study were included for analysis (n = 76).
evidence: This is a direct report of the study's methods, supported by citation to Sebastian et al., 2017.
